Module 6 — Advanced Rendering · Lesson 6.18b

Compute Shaders: GPU Particles

Every program this engine has sent to the GPU went through a rasterizer: vertices in, fragments out, each fragment allowed to write exactly one pixel. This lesson takes the rasterizer away. A compute shader is a function run once per thread over a grid you size yourself, reading and writing any byte of any buffer it is handed — and with that freedom come the problems the rasterizer had been solving for you: the threads at the ragged end of the grid, two structs that mean different bytes to two compilers, randomness with no sequence to draw it from, two threads writing one address, and a flag that silently hands a pass a buffer full of nothing. The vehicle is a particle system of 65,536 sparks that the GPU creates, steps, counts and draws without a byte of it crossing back to the CPU, specified once in C++ so that a harness can run it on both processors and compare every particle. The integers agree bit for bit; the floats agree to within two micrometres after ten simulated seconds; and the frame graph of 6.17 learns what a buffer is, in the process deriving the one flag this lesson would otherwise have had to get right by hand.

1The problem: sixty-five thousand sparks and the bus between them

A grinder throwing sparks, a fountain, rain on a window, embers over a fire, the dust behind a car: each is thousands of tiny, short-lived things that move by simple rules and are drawn as little points of light. They are the classic particle system, and the engine already has every piece you would need to write one the way Module 1 would have. A std::vector of particles; a loop that gives each a velocity and a lifetime when it is born; a loop that adds gravity to the velocity and the velocity to the position every step; a loop that removes the dead. Then, to draw them, copy the whole array into a buffer the GPU can read, with 4.5's gpu_stream_buffer, and issue one instanced draw.

That works, and this lesson builds it — completely, as engine::particle_pool — because it is the thing everything else is compared against. Here is what it costs, measured on this course's machine with the engine built in Release, for a pool of 65,536 particles of which about two thirds are alive at any moment:

  • The step: 0.228 ms. About 3.5 nanoseconds a particle, which is fast: the loop is short, the data is contiguous, and there is nothing in it for the CPU to wait on.
  • The upload: 3.00 MB, every frame, 0.569 ms. Forty-eight bytes a particle — the record §4 designs — whether or not a single particle moved, because the GPU cannot draw what it does not have.

Neither number is alarming at 65,536. Now ask for a million, which a modern game will happily spend on a single explosion. The step becomes 3.75 ms and the upload 6.87 ms: between them 10.6 ms of a 16.7 ms frame, before a single pixel of the scene is drawn. And notice which of the two grew into the problem. It is not the simulation. It is the bus: moving the particles from where they are computed to where they are drawn costs nearly twice as much as computing them. (This machine's GPU shares the CPU's memory, so its "bus" is a copy within one RAM. A discrete GPU pays for the same bytes over PCIe as well.)

Figure 1 draws the two ways out. You could make the CPU faster — threads, SIMD — and it would help the first number and do nothing for the second. Or you could stop moving the particles at all: keep their state in a buffer that lives on the GPU, and have the GPU step it, in place, in the same memory the draw reads. Then the CPU's whole contribution per step is a handful of numbers — this lesson's comes to 144 bytes — describing what the emitter did, and the particles never cross the bus in either direction. The GPU step, measured the same way, is 0.029 ms for 65,536 particles and 0.39 ms for a million.

That requires a way to run arbitrary code on the GPU that is not attached to a triangle. It is called a compute shader, SDL_GPU has supported it since SDL 3.2, and this engine has never written one. And the moment you write one, five things the rasterizer quietly did for you stop happening, and each becomes a section of this lesson:

  • Nobody sizes the work for you. The rasterizer ran the fragment shader once per covered pixel. A compute dispatch runs as many threads as you ask for, in groups whose size is fixed in the shader, and the particle count is not a multiple of the group size. (§3)
  • Data layout becomes your problem. Vertex attributes were described to the pipeline field by field (4.5). A storage buffer is raw bytes, read through a struct declared in two languages and compiled by two compilers — which do not agree about where every field goes. (§4)
  • There is no sequence. A CPU particle system calls a random-number generator in a loop; sixty-five thousand threads running at once cannot share one generator's state. (§5)
  • Threads collide. A fragment wrote only its own pixel. A thread may write anywhere, and the first time two of them count the same thing, most of the counting is lost. (§9)
  • Order is not implied. A render pass's draws land in the order they were issued. Two dispatches in one compute pass are not ordered at all, and a buffer written by one pass and read by the next depends on a flag — cycle — whose wrong value costs every particle you have, every frame. (§10)

There is one more constraint, and it is the course's. CLAUDE.md §4 makes fixed-timestep simulation with render interpolation a law, not a preference. Particles are a simulation. So the GPU must step them at a fixed rate, the draw must interpolate between the last two steps, and §7 counts what that costs a particle system that most engines simply advance by the frame's delta time.

2Building intuition: a draw call with no triangles

Start from what the GPU already does for you, because a compute shader is best understood as that machine with one stage removed. Lesson 4.1 described a draw as a pipeline: vertices are fetched and transformed, triangles are assembled and rasterized, and the rasterizer produces a stream of fragments, each of which runs the fragment shader. The expensive, massively parallel part is the last one — a million fragment-shader invocations for a full-screen triangle — and 4.1's picture of it was lanes in lock-step: 32 or 64 invocations running the same instruction at the same time on different data, many such groups in flight to hide the latency of memory.

The rasterizer's job in all this is scheduling. It decides how many fragment-shader invocations there will be (one per covered pixel), it hands each one its coordinates, and it guarantees where each one's output goes (to its own pixel, blended in draw order). Those are three conveniences, and they are also three restrictions: you cannot run the fragment shader on something that is not a pixel, you cannot choose how many there are, and you cannot write anywhere but your own pixel.

A compute shader is the lanes without the rasterizer. You write a function; you say how many times to run it; each invocation receives an integer identifying which one it is; and it can read and write any element of any storage buffer the pipeline was given. Nothing else. There is no vertex, no primitive, no pixel, no blending, no depth test. If you want an invocation to do something with the 40,961st particle, it has to know it is the 40,961st invocation, and fetch the particle itself.

So the right mental model is not "a new kind of shader" but a for loop whose iterations all run at once: 

// What the CPU particle system does:
for (Uint32 i = 0; i < capacity; ++i) { step_slot(particles[i], i, u); }

// What a compute dispatch of `capacity` threads does, in effect:
//   thread i:  step_slot(particles[i], i, u);      // for every i, simultaneously

and the rule that makes that transformation legal is the one every parallel loop has: no iteration may depend on what another iteration does in the same loop. Iteration i reads particle i and writes particle i, and never touches i + 1. That is true of this lesson's step, and it is the entire reason the step ports to a GPU with no synchronisation at all.

It is not true of every loop a particle system has, and it is worth noticing which one breaks it now, before §9 depends on it. To draw only the living particles you want a list of them, and the obvious CPU loop is 

Uint32 n = 0;
for (Uint32 i = 0; i < capacity; ++i) { if (is_alive(particles[i])) { list[n++] = i; } }

Every iteration reads and writes n. Run those iterations at once and they all read the same n, write their slot to the same place, and increment it by one between them. §9 runs exactly this with a million threads and counts what survives. The fix is a hardware instruction — an atomic — and it is the only place in the lesson the threads have to cooperate.

Hold one more picture from Lesson 1.4, because it decides the shape of the GPU half. The engine's main loop runs the simulation in fixed steps of 1/60 s, zero or more per frame, and the renderer draws the state between the last two steps with a blend factor alpha. On the CPU the steps happen inside on_fixed_step. On the GPU a step is a dispatch, and a dispatch needs a command buffer, which does not exist until the frame begins. So a fixed step on the GPU is recorded — its uniform block written down — and the frame issues one compute pass per recorded step. §12 shows the few lines that do it.

3Threads, groups and the grid

3.1 — A group is the unit of the dispatch

A compute shader does not declare how many threads run it. It declares how many run together: 

[numthreads(64, 1, 1)]
void main(uint3 id : SV_DispatchThreadID) { /* ... */ }

That attribute fixes the size of a thread group at 64. The program then asks for some number of groups — SDL_DispatchGPUCompute(pass, groups_x, groups_y, groups_z) — and the GPU runs groups × 64 threads. The three dimensions are a convenience for work that is naturally two- or three-dimensional, an image or a volume; a particle pool is a list, so everything here is one-dimensional, and the y and z counts are 1.

Why groups at all, rather than just a thread count? Because a group is the unit the hardware schedules onto one of its cores, and threads within a group can share a small fast memory and wait for one another — features this lesson does not use, but which fix the group as the thing that exists physically. The group is also where 4.1's lock-step lanes come from: a group of 64 is run as two SIMD groups of 32 on hardware whose SIMD width is 32 (Apple GPUs and NVIDIA), or one of 64 where the width is 64 (many AMD GPUs). A group size that is a multiple of 64 wastes no lanes on any of them, which is the whole of why 64 is the conventional choice.

3.2 — Three IDs, and the one you want

Each thread can ask where it is in three ways. SV_GroupID is which group it belongs to; SV_GroupThreadID is its place within that group, 0 to 63; SV_DispatchThreadID is its place in the whole grid,

\[ \texttt{SV\_DispatchThreadID}.x = \texttt{SV\_GroupID}.x \times 64 + \texttt{SV\_GroupThreadID}.x \] dispatch id = group id x 64 + thread-in-group id

and that last one is the particle's slot. Thread 3 of group 2 is thread 2·64 + 3 = 131 of the dispatch, and it steps particle 131. Figure 2 draws the grid for 1,000 particles.

3.3 — The tail

Now size the dispatch. 1,000 particles at 64 a group is 15.625 groups, and there is no such thing as five-eighths of a group. So you ask for sixteen — the ceiling of the division — and the GPU runs 1,024 threads. Threads 1,000 to 1,023 exist, run the shader, compute a slot number, and there is no particle there.

What happens next depends entirely on the first line of the shader. With it: 

if (slot >= capacity) { return; }

the twenty-four idle threads do nothing. Without it they read and write past the end of the buffer. What lies there is undefined — on some backends the access is simply dropped, on others it lands in whatever memory follows — and the harness does not try the undefined case. Instead particles_probe.comp.hlsl runs the unguarded write into a buffer with a guard zone after the data, and counts: 24 writes past the end of a 1,000-element array, one per idle thread, every time (§H). Every kernel in this lesson begins with the check. The engine's pools are always powers of two of at least 64, so today the tail is empty; the check costs one comparison and is the one line nobody may delete, because the day somebody changes the pool size it is all that stands between the tail and the next buffer in memory.

3.4 — The ceiling, done carefully

The textbook ceiling division is (n + 63) / 64. It is correct for every n that anybody will ever dispatch, and wrong at the edge: for n within 63 of 232 the addition wraps, and (4,294,967,295 + 63) / 64 is zero groups (§B's control). engine::groups_for is written as n / 64 + (n % 64 != 0), which cannot wrap, and returns 67,108,864. No particle pool reaches four billion. The point is that a helper's job is to close an edge rather than document one, and that the fix costs nothing.

4Storage buffers: a layout two compilers agree on

4.1 — What a particle is

Before any buffer, decide what one particle holds. The simulation needs a position, a velocity, an age and a life span; the draw needs a position and enough to decide how the particle looks. Three more requirements pin the rest down:

  • Interpolation needs the previous position. Lesson 1.4's renderer draws lerp(previous, current, alpha), so the state must carry where the particle was at the start of the last step. That is twelve bytes a particle that an engine advancing by the frame's delta time would not pay — the fixed-step law, costed.
  • Variation needs a name. Sparks of slightly different sizes and brightnesses look like sparks; identical ones look like a texture. Rather than store a size and a tint, the particle stores its serial number — which birth it was — and the draw hashes that into whatever variation it wants (§5). Four bytes buy unlimited per-particle variety.
  • Dead must be representable, and cheap. A particle is alive while age < life. A record of all zeros has age 0 and life 0, so it is dead, and a buffer cleared to zero is a pool with nothing in it.

That is twelve floats' worth of data: three vec3s and three scalars. The question is how to arrange them, and it is not a question of taste.

4.2 — The tempting struct, and what it becomes

Take a smaller version first, because it shows the whole problem: 

struct Naive { float3 position; float3 velocity; float age; };

In C++, with the engine's vec3 of three floats, that is 28 bytes: position at 0, velocity at 12, age at 24. HLSL's own rules for a structured buffer — tightly packed, which is what DXC produces when it compiles to DXIL for Direct3D — agree: 12 and 24, stride 28. (That one is stated from Microsoft's packing rules rather than measured: this machine's shadercross has no DXC, 4.3's capability probe says so at configure time, and CI's Windows job is where it would be checked.) Now compile the same HLSL the way this course's toolchain does on macOS — glslang's HLSL front end, producing SPIR-V, which shadercross turns into MSL — and ask the SPIR-V where the fields went. spirv-dis on the compiled kernel says: 

OpMemberDecorate %Naive 0 Offset 0
OpMemberDecorate %Naive 1 Offset 16
OpMemberDecorate %Naive 2 Offset 28
OpDecorate %_runtimearr_Naive ArrayStride 32

Velocity at 16, age at 28, and a stride of 32. The SPIR-V rules this front end applies to a storage buffer give a three-component vector the alignment of a four-component one — sixteen bytes — so velocity cannot start at 12 and is pushed to 16. The same HLSL file describes two different memory layouts depending on which compiler reads it, and the C++ struct matches only one of them.

It is worth seeing the failure rather than imagining it, so verify_618b §A does exactly that. The probe kernel writes position = (1, 2, 3), velocity = (4, 5, 6), age = 7 into a buffer of Naive records; the harness reads the bytes back and looks at them through the C++ struct. It finds velocity = (0, 4, 5) and age = 6: the padding's zero, then two of the velocity's components, then the third one mistaken for the age. Nothing crashes and nothing warns. Every particle simply moves in the wrong direction at the wrong speed, and a second record starts four bytes later than C++ thinks, so the error is different for every particle in the buffer.

SDL knows about this. The documentation of its buffer usage flags says that storage data must follow std140 conventions, and spells out the practical consequence: "vec3 and vec4 fields are 16-byte aligned". That is the rule, and Figure 3 draws what it means.

4.3 — Three rows

The layout every compiler agrees on is one in which the question never arises: every float3 starts on a 16-byte boundary and is followed by exactly one four-byte scalar, so each float3-plus-scalar pair is one 16-byte row with no padding for anybody to disagree about. The particle has three vec3s and three scalars, and they pair up exactly: 

struct particle
{
    vec3 position{};   float age = 0.0f;      // row 0: bytes  0..15
    vec3 velocity{};   float life = 0.0f;     // row 1: bytes 16..31
    vec3 previous{};   Uint32 serial = 0;     // row 2: bytes 32..47
};
static_assert(sizeof(particle) == 48, "must match `Particle` in the particle shaders");

and particles.hpp static_asserts every one of the six offsets. The harness then checks the other half: the probe writes a Particle with the values 1 to 12 in its fields and finds them at C++'s offsets, the next record at byte 48, and the uint in row 2 arriving as the bits of 12 (§A). The two static assertions and the readback are the only things standing between a struct edited in one language and a simulation that is quietly wrong in the other — which is why 6.17b's light record was built of float4s for the same reason, and why this one is built of rows.

Note

"Just use float4 everywhere" is the other common answer, and it is equally safe. Rows are preferred here because they waste nothing: a particle as three float4s with unused fourth components would need its three scalars somewhere else. The rule to carry away is not "rows" but never let a compiler choose padding. If the layout has padding, write it as a named field on both sides.

4.4 — Where the buffers go: a third register layout

Lesson 4.3 met SDL_GPU's rule that a shader's resources must sit in particular registers, and Lesson 6.17b met it again when the fragment stage got its first storage buffer at t8, space2. Compute pipelines have a layout of their own, stated in SDL_gpu.h above SDL_CreateGPUComputePipeline (checked at 3.4.12):

Resource registers by stage in SDL_GPU's HLSL layout
StageTextures and read-only storageRead-write storageUniforms
vertext[n], space0— (none)b[n], space1
fragmentt[n], space2— (none)b[n], space3
computet[n], space0u[n], space1b[n], space2

Two things in that table are new. A compute shader is the only stage that can write a buffer: the graphics stages read storage and never write it, which is why the u column is empty for them. And a compute shader's uniform block is b0 in space2 — the space in which a fragment shader keeps its textures. It is the one number in this lesson that a muscle memory trained on graphics shaders will get wrong, and the symptom is a pipeline that creates, dispatches and computes with a uniform block full of zeros.

The read-write buffers are also bound differently. A read-only storage buffer is bound by a call inside the pass, SDL_BindGPUComputeStorageBuffers, like every binding the engine has made so far. A read-write buffer is not: it is named when the pass begins, SDL_BeginGPUComputePass(cb, textures, n, buffers, m), as an array whose index is the shader's u register. The reason is that the backend has to know, at the start of the pass, every resource the pass will write, so it can place the barriers that make those writes safe to read afterwards (§10). A read-write buffer is, to a compute pass, what an attachment is to a render pass — and §11 makes the frame graph treat it exactly that way.

4.5 — Six numbers where there were four

And the counts. SDL_GPUShaderCreateInfo asked for four numbers — samplers, storage textures, storage buffers, uniform buffers — and 4.3 read them out of shadercross's JSON so nobody had to count by hand. SDL_GPUComputePipelineCreateInfo asks for six, because it distinguishes read-only storage from read-write, plus the thread-group size, which "should match the value in the shader". shadercross reports all nine; for the step kernel: 

{ "samplers": 0, "readonly_storage_textures": 0, "readonly_storage_buffers": 0,
  "readwrite_storage_textures": 0, "readwrite_storage_buffers": 1, "uniform_buffers": 1,
  "threadcount_x": 64, "threadcount_y": 1, "threadcount_z": 1 }

Hand that file to 4.3's parse_shader_reflection and it refuses — correctly. The parser searches for each key with its quotes, and "storage_buffers" is not a key in a compute reflection; "readonly_storage_buffers" contains the letters but not the opening quote. A parser that had searched without quotes would have read the wrong count and succeeded, which is the bug 4.3 designed the quoting against, meeting a case 4.3 never saw. The new parse_compute_reflection sits beside it in gpu_shader.cpp, uses the same scanner, and demands all nine keys. The harness checks both refusals: each parser rejects the other's JSON (§B).

And there is no compute shader object to create. SDL_GPU builds a graphics pipeline out of two SDL_GPUShaders and fifty-odd fields of fixed-function state; a compute pipeline has no fixed-function state, so it is created straight from the code. That is why the new gpu_compute_pipeline owns a pipeline and nothing else, and why its load is gpu_shader::load with the stage decided for it — including 4.3's trap that under MSL the entry point is main0, which a kernel does not escape.

5Randomness without a sequence

5.1 — Why a generator does not port

Every random-number generator you have used is a sequence: a state, and a function that advances it. std::mt19937 holds 2.5 KB of state; the tiny linear congruential generator Numerical Recipes printed holds 32 bits and advances with x = x · 1664525 + 1013904223. Either way the n-th number depends on the n − 1 before it, and a CPU particle system that calls next() in its spawn loop gets a different number for each particle because the calls happen one after another.

Sixty-five thousand threads do not happen one after another. If they share one generator, every next() is a read-modify-write of the same state — §2's broken counting loop, with randomness as the thing being lost. If each thread keeps its own generator, each generator needs a seed, and the seed must differ per thread; and a seed that is just the thread's index is where the trouble starts.

The way out is to stop thinking of a random number as the next value of a sequence and start thinking of it as a hash of a name. A particle has a name — its serial number, which birth it was — and a function that scrambles 32 bits into 32 bits so thoroughly that neighbouring inputs give unrelated outputs turns that name into as many random numbers as the particle needs. No state is shared, nothing depends on the order the threads run in, and — the property the rest of this lesson leans on — the same name gives the same numbers on any processor that performs the same integer arithmetic, which all of them do exactly.

5.2 — Three generators that are not random

The question is which scrambling function. §C of the harness measures four candidates by the thing a spark actually uses: pairs. A spark's direction is two draws, so the test is whether the pair of numbers particle i draws, (u2i, u2i+1), fills the unit square, and whether particle i's first number tells you anything about particle i + 1's. Figure 4 plots 2,048 pairs from each of three.

One LCG step, seeded by the index. The natural first attempt: seed a tiny generator with the particle's index, take one step, use the result. But an LCG is linear — seed i + 1's output is seed i's plus the constant 1,664,525 — so consecutive particles get numbers that differ by the same amount every time. Measured over 65,536 particles: the correlation between neighbours is +0.9977, and the pairs reach 128 of 4,096 cells of a 64 × 64 grid: every pair lies on one diagonal line, because each number is the one before it plus 1,664,525/232. A fountain built on it would emit its sparks in a slowly rotating pattern that looks like a bug in the emitter, not in the random numbers.

The shader folklore hash, fract(sin(x) × 43758.5453), found in thousands of shaders. It fills the square — all 4,096 cells, correlation +0.0014 for small inputs — and it has two defects that no scatter plot at this scale shows. The first is that it has almost no bits. The product sin(x) × 43758.5453 is up to 43,758 in magnitude, and a float keeps 24 significant bits: between 32,768 and 65,536 the gap between representable floats is 215 − 23 = 1/256, so fract() of anything in that range is a multiple of 1/256. Most products land above 2,048, where the gap is at least 1/4,096 — so the function can only return about four thousand distinct values. Measured: 4,178 distinct outputs from 65,536 inputs, about twelve bits of randomness where the output format holds twenty-four. The second defect appears for large inputs: above 224, float(i) cannot represent odd integers, so particle i and particle i + 1 are the same input half the time, and the neighbour correlation jumps to +0.4963. A serial number passes 224 after fourteen minutes of a 20,000-a-second fountain.

And a third defect, which only a two-processor harness can see: it is not one function. sin on a GPU is a fast approximation, not the correctly-rounded library call of the CPU, and multiplying by 43,758 magnifies the last-bit differences into the visible digits. The probe kernel evaluates the same expression for the first 220 integers: 480,168 of 1,048,576 outputs differ from C++'s, and 1,246 by more than 0.01. A particle system built on it has no CPU reference at all.

PCG's hash. Jarzynski and Olano's "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering" (JCGT 2020) measured many candidates for exactly this use and recommended one built from Melissa O'Neill's PCG generator: one LCG step to advance a state, followed by PCG's output permutation, which uses the state's own top bits to choose a shift and so destroys the linearity that ruined the first candidate. The engine's version is four lines of integer arithmetic, identical in C++ and HLSL: 

[[nodiscard]] constexpr Uint32 pcg_hash(Uint32 input)
{
    const Uint32 state = input * 747796405u + 2891336453u;
    const Uint32 word = ((state >> ((state >> 28u) + 4u)) ^ state) * 277803737u;
    return (word >> 22u) ^ word;
}

Measured: neighbour correlation −0.0019, every one of the 4,096 cells reached, a χ² of 4,198 against 4,095 degrees of freedom, and 65,411 distinct values among 65,536 — which is itself a check, because a perfectly random 24-bit output should collide about 65,536² / (2 · 224) = 128 times, leaving 65,408. And the property the whole lesson rests on: run it on the GPU for 1,048,576 consecutive inputs and every output is identical to C++'s, bit for bit. Integer multiplication, shifts and exclusive-or have exactly one correct answer, and both processors produce it.

5.3 — From bits to a float, exactly

A hash gives 32 random bits; a spark wants a number in [0, 1). The obvious conversion, float(h) / 4294967295.0f, has two roundings in it — 32 bits into a float's 24, then a division a GPU compiler is permitted to approximate — and either can make the two processors disagree. The engine takes the top 24 bits instead: 

[[nodiscard]] constexpr float unit_float(Uint32 bits)
{
    return static_cast<float>(bits >> 8u) * (1.0f / 16777216.0f);
}

An integer below 224 is represented by a float exactly, and 1/16,777,216 is 2−24, a power of two, so the multiplication only changes the exponent. There is no rounding anywhere, and the harness confirms it: the same million floats, bit for bit, on both processors (§C). The result is a multiple of 2−24 in [0, 1 − 2−24], which is every value a float can hold at that spacing.

5.4 — A particle's stream

A spark needs four numbers at birth: two for its direction, one for its speed, one for its life span. It gets them by hashing its name once and then hashing the hash: 

particle_rng rng(serial, seed);     // state = pcg_hash(serial ^ seed)
const float u_cos   = rng.next();   // state = pcg_hash(state); return unit_float(state)
const float u_phi   = rng.next();
const float u_speed = rng.next();
const float u_life  = rng.next();

The emitter's seed selects which fountain — two emitters with different seeds produce unrelated sparks from the same serial numbers — and the order of the four draws is part of the specification: the kernel draws them in the same sequence, so the third number means "speed" on both processors. Reorder the lines in one file and the harness reports every particle wrong while every individual function is still correct.

5.5 — A direction uniform over a cone

The fountain emits into a cone around its axis, half-angle θmax = 0.35 radians (20°). "A random direction in the cone" sounds like "a random angle between 0 and θmax and a random turn around the axis", and that is wrong, for a reason you can see before you compute anything. Look down the cone's axis at the patch of the unit sphere it cuts out — a cap — and draw rings at equal steps of angle. The rings near the rim are long and the ones near the axis are short, because a ring at angle θ has circumference 2π sin θ. Choose the angle uniformly and you put as many directions in the tiny innermost ring as in the long outer one: the density per unit area climbs toward the axis. Figure 5, left, shows it: a bright core where a real fountain has none.

What we want is equal density per unit area of the cap. The area of a strip of the unit sphere between θ and θ + dθ, all the way around, is its circumference times its width, 2π sin θ dθ. Integrate from the axis to θ and the area of the cap is

\[ A(\theta) = \int_0^{\theta} 2\pi \sin\theta'\,d\theta' = 2\pi\,(1 - \cos\theta) \] A(theta) = 2 pi (1 - cos theta)

so the fraction of the whole cap that lies within angle θ is (1 − cos θ) / (1 − cos θmax). For the directions to be uniform by area, that fraction must equal a uniform random number u, which gives the recipe directly:

\[ 1 - \cos\theta = u\,(1 - \cos\theta_{\max}), \qquad \phi = 2\pi v \] 1 - cos(theta) = u * (1 - cos(theta_max)) ; phi = 2 pi v

— uniform in cos θ, not in θ. A worked number, with the demo's cone: the cap has height 1 − cos 0.35 = 0.0606. The median sample, u = 0.5, has 1 − cos θ = 0.0303, so cos θ = 0.9697 and θ = 0.2469 rad (14.1°). Uniform in angle would have put the median at 0.175 rad: half of all sparks within 10° of the axis instead of within 14°, which is the bright core of Figure 5.

Then the sine, and a trap worth naming because it recurs through the rest of the course: sin θ is sqrt(1 − cos²θ) on paper and in the obvious code, and for a narrow cone cos θ is close to 1, so the subtraction cancels away most of the digits that mattered. Write h = 1 − cos θ — which the sampling formula hands you directly, without ever forming cos θ — and

\[ \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - (1-h)^2} = \sqrt{h\,(2 - h)} \] sin(theta) = sqrt(h * (2 - h))

has no subtraction near 1 anywhere. For the median sample: √(0.0303 × 1.9697) = 0.2443. The direction is then assembled in a frame around the axis: tangent · sin θ cos φ + bitangent · sin θ sin φ + axis · cos θ. The tangent and bitangent come from Duff and colleagues' branch-free construction (JCGT 2017), because the textbook one — cross the axis with "up" — divides by zero when the axis is up, which for a fountain is the only axis anybody uses. And they are computed once, on the CPU, into the uniform block, because they are the same for every particle; that rule — a number that is the same for every thread is computed once, never sixty-five thousand times — shapes the block in §7.

6Emission: a clock and a ring

6.1 — The fraction

An emitter emits at a rate, 20,000 particles a second, and the simulation runs in fixed steps of 1/60 s, so each step should emit 333.33 particles. Truncate that to 333 and the fountain loses a third of a particle every step — twenty a second, 1,200 a minute, a rate that is silently 0.1% low forever. The fix is a clock that accumulates the rate and pays out whole births, carrying the fraction: 

carry_ += rate * h;                  // 0.33 + 333.33 = 333.67
const double whole = floor(carry_);  // 333 births this step
carry_ -= whole;                     // 0.67 carried to the next

and the step pattern becomes 333, 333, 334, repeating. Measured over one simulated minute: exactly 1,200,000 births — 333 on 2,400 steps and 334 on 1,200 — against 1,198,800 for truncation (§D).

The clock keeps its fraction in a double, and it is worth being exact about why, because the first version of particles.hpp gave a reason the harness then refused. It said a float accumulator would lose its fractional digits after 224 births. It would not: the clock subtracts the whole part every step, so it never holds more than 334.34, and over a simulated hour a float carry and a double carry differ by one birth. What actually limits the clock is the step itself: 1/60 is not a float, the nearest one is 0.0166666675, and at that step both carries emit 72,000,002 or 72,000,003 particles an hour where the arithmetic says 72,000,000. The double costs eight bytes per emitter and removes the question, and the header now says so.

6.2 — A pool is a ring

Where do the new particles go? The CPU answer — append to a vector, erase the dead — is exactly what a GPU is bad at: appending needs a shared counter and erasing reshuffles everything. The answer this engine uses needs neither. The pool has a fixed capacity, a power of two, and particle number s — its serial, counting births from zero — lives in slot

\[ \text{slot}(s) = s \mathbin{\&} (\text{capacity} - 1) \] slot(s) = s AND (capacity - 1) — which is s mod capacity, for a power of two

so births walk round the pool like a clock hand, and each new particle replaces whatever was capacity births ago — the oldest particle in the pool, which with a long enough pool is long dead. A step's births are serials first to first + count − 1, a contiguous arc of the ring. Figure 6 draws a pool of sixteen where serials 13 to 17 are born: slots 13, 14, 15, 0 and 1.

The kernel runs one thread per slot, not per birth, and each thread asks: does this step's arc include my slot? Its distance forward from the arc's first slot is (slot − first) & mask — unsigned subtraction wraps, which is exactly "forward round the ring" — and the slot is born this step if that distance is below count. If it is, the thread spawns serial first + d; if not, it steps whatever lives there. No thread communicates with any other. That is the whole of why a ring suits a GPU, and why this lesson's emitter needs no atomics at all.

6.3 — Why a power of two, and what "long enough" means

Serials are 32-bit and they wrap: at 20,000 a second, 232 births take 59.7 hours. With a mask the wrap is invisible — 4,294,967,295 lives in slot 1,023 of a 1,024-slot pool and 0 lives in slot 0, consecutive as they should be — because 1,024 divides 232. With a pool of 1,000 and s % 1000 the same two serials land in slots 295 and 0, and the ring's one invariant — the next birth replaces the oldest particle — breaks, once every two and a half days. §D prints both sequences across the wrap; Figure 6's table is that output.

"Long enough" is a single inequality. A slot comes round every capacity / rate seconds, and a particle that lives longer than that is replaced while still alive. The fountain's longest life is 3 s, and 65,536 / 20,000 = 3.28 s, so nothing is cut short: §D runs 200,000 births and counts zero live particles overwritten. Halve the pool and a slot comes round every 1.64 s: 152,704 of 200,000 particles — 76.4% — are replaced before their time, losing 0.685 s of life on average. It looks like a fountain whose sparks vanish in mid-air at a height that has nothing to do with gravity.

Note

The ring's price is that a particle's death is decided twice: by its own clock, and by the ring coming round. The alternative, used by many production systems since Gareth Thomas's GDC 2014 talk on compute-based particles, is a dead list: a stack of free slot indices that births pop from and deaths push to, which recycles exactly the dead and nothing else. It needs two atomics per particle per frame and it makes the order of births depend on the order of deaths, which varies run to run — so it has no bit-exact CPU twin. The ring is deterministic, atomic-free and exactly reproducible, which is what a lesson that compares two processors needs. Exercise 5 builds the dead list and measures the difference.

6.4 — Births belong somewhere in the step

A step of 1/60 s emits 333 particles, and it is tempting to give them all age zero at the emitter. Physically they were born at different instants during that sixtieth of a second — the first early, the last just now — and by the end of the step the early ones should already be a little way out. Put them all at the emitter and every step's births travel together as a shell, and shells from successive steps sit one step's travel apart: at 7 m/s, 11.7 cm. The fountain comes out in layers, as if pumped rather than poured.

Where exactly does birth k belong? The clock held the fraction c when the step began and rises at rate per second, so during the step it reads c + rate · t. Each birth happens as it crosses a whole number: birth 0 when it reaches 1, birth k when it reaches k + 1. Solving,

\[ t_k = \frac{k + 1 - c}{\text{rate}}, \qquad \text{age}_k = h - t_k = h - (k + 1 - c)\cdot\frac{1}{\text{rate}} \] t_k = (k + 1 - c) / rate ; age_k = h - (k + 1 - c) * inv_rate

Worked, for a step that begins with c = 1/3 at 20,000 a second: birth 0 happens (1 − 0.3333)/20,000 = 33.3 µs into the step and is 16.63 ms old at its end; birth 332 happens at (333 − 0.3333)/20,000 = 16.63 ms and is 33.3 µs old. The clock reaches 333.67 by the step's end, so there is no birth 333 until next step — the same 333 the clock paid out. The kernel spawns each particle and then advances it by its own age in a single step of that length, so it is where it would be had it really been born then. inv_rate is in the uniform block rather than a division in the kernel, so both processors multiply by the same float.

That is the theory, and the measurement then refused half of what this section first predicted about it. §E runs the fountain twice — births spread through the step, and all at the step's end — and measures how lumpy the heights of young particles are (the average change between neighbouring 5 mm height bins, over the average count). With the demo's own emitter, speeds from 4 to 7 m/s, the two came out 0.232 and 0.221: no shells to speak of either way. The reason is in the speeds. A step's births leave at speeds 3 m/s apart, so after t seconds they are spread over 3t metres — wider than the shell spacing by the second step. The spread of speeds erases the shells by itself. Narrow the speeds to 6.9–7.0 m/s, as an emitter of identical droplets or tracer rounds would, and the prediction holds: 0.912 against 0.213. Figure 7 is that case.

So spreading births through the step is not always visible, and it is still right: it costs one multiply-add per birth, it is what the physics says, and it is the difference between an emitter that works for every speed distribution and one that works for the distribution it was tuned on.

7The step: semi-implicit Euler, implicit drag, and a floor

7.1 — Velocity first

Lesson 1.3 met this integrator in a sidebar: swap the two lines of the obvious update — change the velocity first, then move with the new velocity — and you get semi-implicit Euler, which conserves energy far better in anything that oscillates, and which 1.3 promised proper treatment in Module 8. Lesson 8.1 will give it that treatment; here it is simply the right default, and the particle step is two lines of it: 

p.velocity = (p.velocity + u.gravity * dt) * inv_drag;   // velocity first...
p.position = p.position + p.velocity * dt;               // ...then move with the new one

7.2 — Drag, implicitly

Sparks slow down in air, and the simplest model is linear drag: an acceleration opposing the velocity in proportion to it, dv/dt = g − kv. The explicit step evaluates the drag at the old velocity:

\[ \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{v} + (\mathbf{g} - k\mathbf{v})\,h = (1 - kh)\,\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{g}h \] v' = v + (g - k v) h = (1 - k h) v + g h

and that factor (1 − kh) is where it can go wrong. If kh exceeds 1 the factor is negative, so the velocity flips sign every step; if kh exceeds 2 its magnitude exceeds 1, and the flipping grows. Evaluate the drag at the new velocity instead — the implicit choice — and solve:

\[ \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{v} + (\mathbf{g} - k\mathbf{v}')\,h \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbf{v}'\,(1 + kh) = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{g}h \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbf{v}' = \frac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{g}h}{1 + kh} \] v' = (v + g h) / (1 + k h)

The factor 1/(1 + kh) is between 0 and 1 for every positive k and h: the velocity decays, whatever the step. §F makes the difference concrete with a thick medium, k = 150/s, at the engine's step (kh = 2.5), starting from 1 m/s: after ten explicit steps the speed is 57.67 m/s (1.510, alternating in sign); after ten implicit steps it is 3.63 × 10−6 m/s (3.5−10). At the demo's k = 0.4/s the two agree to 4.4 × 10−5 of the velocity per step, so the implicit form costs nothing where the explicit one works and saves you where it does not. The factor for a full step, 1/(1 + kh), is the same for every particle, so it too is computed once on the CPU and sent in the uniform block as inv_drag_h; only a birth's pre-age step, whose length varies, computes its own.

7.3 — The floor

A particle that ends a step below the plane y = ground while moving down bounces: 

if (p.position.y < u.ground && p.velocity.y < 0.0f)
{
    p.position.y = u.ground;                          // back onto the surface
    p.velocity.y = -p.velocity.y * u.restitution;     // the normal speed, reversed and reduced
    p.velocity.x = p.velocity.x * u.keep;             // the tangential speed, reduced by friction
    p.velocity.z = p.velocity.z * u.keep;
}

Each clause has a reason. Only while moving down: a particle that bounced last step may still be below the plane this step on its way back up, and bouncing it again would send it back down through the floor. Back onto the surface: a step that overshoots by 3 cm leaves the particle 3 cm under the floor for a frame, and the depth test then hides it — a flicker at every impact. Normal and tangential separately: restitution is how much of the speed into the surface survives, friction how much of the speed along it does, and they are different physical things (Lesson 8.9 builds both properly for rigid bodies).

How much height should a bounce keep? Kinetic energy is ½mv², the height a particle rises to is v²/2g, and the bounce multiplies v by the restitution e — so it multiplies the height by e². At e = 0.45 each bounce should keep 0.2025 of the last one's height. §F drops a particle from 1 m and measures peaks of 0.1848, 0.0318 and 0.0033 m: ratios of 0.185, 0.172 and 0.103. The prediction held for the first bounce and failed, worse and worse, for the later ones — and the failure has a formula.

A semi-implicit step launched upward at speed v0 reaches, after n steps, a height of Σj=1..n (v0 − jgh)h, whose maximum is

\[ y_{\max} \approx \frac{v_0^2}{2g} - \frac{v_0 h}{2} \] y_max ~ v0^2 / (2 g) - v0 h / 2

— the true height less half a step's travel. As a fraction of the true height the shortfall is gh/v0, which grows as the bounce shrinks. For the first bounce v0 ≈ 0.45 × √(2 · 9.81) = 1.99 m/s, so the shortfall is 9.81 × (1/60) / 1.99 = 8.2%, and 0.2025 × (1 − 0.082) = 0.186 — within 0.001 of the measured 0.1848. The third bounce is 3 mm high and lasts three steps; a step that size cannot resolve it at all. The control that proves the diagnosis is the same drop at a quarter of the step: peaks of 0.1970, 0.0386 and 0.0070, ratios 0.197, 0.196 and 0.181, all moving toward e² (Figure 8). It is the step's error, not a bug — and it is the same first-order error Lesson 1.3 measured for a fall, which is one reason Module 8 spends a lesson on integrators.

7.4 — Why state, and not a formula

It is worth asking whether a particle needs a simulation at all, because for a long time GPU particle systems did without one. With gravity and no floor, a particle's position is a closed form, p(t) = p0 + v0t + ½gt², and a vertex shader can evaluate it from the particle's birth time, direction and speed — all of which are hashes of its serial number. No buffer, no step, no compute. §F confirms it would even be more accurate than the step: after one second the stepped height is 0.0817 m off the formula, which is semi-implicit Euler's first-order error ght/2 = 0.0818 m.

The floor ends that. When a particle bounces depends on where it was, which depends on when it last bounced, and each bounce changes the velocity that decides the next one. That is a history — piecewise, and still solvable for one plane, but the moment the floor is uneven, or the particles collide with the depth buffer (Exercise 4), or a wind field varies over space and time, there is no formula left to evaluate. State is what you keep when the future depends on the past in a way you cannot write down, and a compute shader is how you step state on the GPU.

7.5 — Between two steps

The draw interpolates each particle between previous — its position at the start of the last step — and its current position, with Lesson 1.4's alpha. One detail makes that correct for a ring. When a slot is respawned, previous is set to the emitter, not left holding the old tenant's position. Leave it, and for one frame the new spark is drawn somewhere on the line from where the dead one was to the emitter — a streak across the screen, once per birth, sixty times a second, and indistinguishable from a rendering bug. The rule is the one 1.4 gave for any interpolated state: previous must always be a position of this object.

8Drawing without vertices

8.1 — A billboard from two IDs

A spark is drawn as a small square that always faces the camera — a billboard — shaded into a soft disc. Every vertex the engine has drawn so far came from a vertex buffer, described field by field to the pipeline in 4.5. A billboard's four corners are not data anybody stored; they are a function of the particle and the camera. So the particle pipeline has no vertex buffer at all, and its vertex shader has no inputs. It is invoked six times per instance — two triangles — and it finds everything from its two system values:

  • SV_InstanceID says which particle. It indexes the list of living slots (§9), which gives the slot, which indexes the pool.
  • SV_VertexID says which corner: an index into a six-entry table of (±1, ±1), in counter-clockwise order as seen by the camera — the course's front face (conventions §7), so the default back-face cull keeps them.

The corner is then placed in the camera's own plane: 

const float3 centre = lerp(p.previous, p.position, alpha);
const float3 world  = centre + (right * c.x + up * c.y) * radius;

where right and up are the camera's axes in world space. They are free: Lesson 2.9 built look_at so that the view matrix's rotation rows are the camera's axes, and a rotation's inverse is its transpose, so row 0 is the world direction the view maps to +x and row 1 the one it maps to +y. Worked, with the demo's shot camera at (3.7633, 2.3, 6.1382) looking at (0, 1.3, 0): camera_right returns (0.8525, 0, −0.5227), camera_up returns (−0.0719, 0.9905, −0.1173), and the view matrix maps them to exactly (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0) — computed by the engine's own look_at. A spark at (0.10, 1.00, 0.20) with radius 0.03 puts corner v2, (1, 1), at (0.1234, 1.0297, 0.1808). Figure 9 draws the chain and the quad.

Everything the spark looks like comes from two numbers the pool already holds: its age as a fraction of its life, and its serial. The fraction shrinks it and cools it — white-yellow at birth to deep orange at death, fading on a square so the end is a fade rather than a pop — and a hash of the serial varies its size and brightness between 0.6 and 1.4 of nominal. None of that needs a byte of storage, which is §4's four-byte serial paying for itself.

8.2 — Storage buffers in the vertex stage

The vertex shader reads two storage buffers — the pool at t0 and the list at t1, both in space 0, the vertex stage's texture-and-storage space from §4's table — bound with SDL_BindGPUVertexStorageBuffers. The graphics stages can only read storage, so both are declared StructuredBuffer, not RWStructuredBuffer, and both buffers need the GRAPHICS_STORAGE_READ usage bit in addition to their compute bits. Miss that bit and the bind fails validation; miss a compute bit and the kernel's does. gpu_particles::create argues every bit in a comment, because the usage flags are where most of the ways to get this wrong live.

8.3 — Added to the light, tested against the scene

Sparks emit light, and light adds, so the pipeline blends with 6.13's blend_add(): destination += source. That has a consequence that §9 depends on — addition commutes, so the particles can be drawn in any order at all, up to a rounding §9 measures — and it decides where the draw goes: into the HDR target, before the tonemap, because a spark is a quantity of light like any other surface (6.12) and because a spark bright enough should bloom (6.13). The overlay of 6.18 went after the tonemap for the opposite reason; the line between scene-referred and display-referred is the one 6.18 drew, and sparks are on the scene side.

The draw is tested against the scene's depth and does not write it. The test hides sparks behind geometry; the write would make each spark hide the ones behind it — and since the list's order changes every frame (§9), which sparks were hidden would change every frame too. That is Lesson 6.11's rule for blended geometry, arrived at from a different direction. §K checks the test with a depth attachment cleared to the device depth of a plane: in front of every spark (2.89 m from the camera, the nearest spark being 3.09 m out) it leaves zero lit pixels; through the fountain's axis at 6 m, with 21,611 of 43,248 sparks behind it, it leaves 45.9% of the light — and 9,401 of the 10,329 lit pixels, because nearly every pixel the far half covered, the near half covers too.

9Counting on a GPU

9.1 — The number nobody on the CPU knows

The draw of §8 needs one number: how many instances. That is the count of living particles, and it exists nowhere. The ring decides births and the particles' own clocks decide deaths, both on the GPU, so after a step the CPU has no idea how many are alive. It could draw every slot — 65,536 instances, the dead ones collapsed to nothing in the vertex shader — and pay for about 20,000 wasted billboards a frame. It could read the pool back and count, which is a download of the 3 MB this lesson exists to stop moving, followed by a stall: the CPU waits for the GPU to finish, and the GPU then waits for the CPU to issue the next frame. Or it could read back only the count, a frame late, and draw last frame's number of particles against this frame's list.

None of those is necessary, because SDL_GPU, like every modern API, can take a draw's arguments from a buffer. SDL_DrawGPUPrimitivesIndirect(pass, buffer, offset, count) reads an SDL_GPUIndirectDrawCommand — four Uint32s: vertices, instances, first vertex, first instance — from the buffer when the GPU reaches the draw. If a compute pass earlier in the same frame wrote the instance count into that buffer, the draw uses it, and the number was produced, consumed and forgotten on the GPU. The CPU issues a draw whose size it never learns.

That leaves the problem of producing the count, and a list of the living slots for the vertex shader to index — §2's broken loop.

9.2 — The lost update

Here is that loop's increment written as a kernel, as literally as possible, in the probe: 

words[0] = words[0] + 1u;   // every thread, once

Run it with 1,048,576 threads and read words[0] back. Fifteen trials across five runs of the harness counted between 296 and 509. Over 99.9% of the increments vanished, and the survivors are a different number each time.

The line is three operations — read the value, add one, write the result — and nothing stops another thread from reading between the first and the third. Two threads that both read 7 both write 8: two increments, one counted (Figure 10). On a GPU it is worse than on a multicore CPU, because of 4.1's lock-step: the 32 lanes of a SIMD group execute the read together, see the same value, and write the same result, so a whole group contributes one increment at best, and many groups are in flight at once doing the same. The number that survives says how the hardware happened to schedule the groups, which is why it changes from run to run and why it is not a number to reason with.

The fix is an instruction that performs all three steps as one indivisible operation on the memory itself — an atomic: 

uint before;
InterlockedAdd(words[0], 1u, before);   // before = the value this thread replaced

With it the count is 1,048,576, every time (§H). And before is the part that turns a count into a list: each thread receives the value it replaced, which is a number no other thread received. It is this thread's place.

Atomics are not free. Every thread in the grid that performs one on the same address is serialised on that address, so a million threads adding to one counter wait on each other a million times. For this lesson's two-thirds-alive pool that is about 45,000 atomics a frame, which the measured compaction absorbs (§L's GPU step includes it). A production system at a million particles reduces it: a SIMD group counts its own survivors with a wave intrinsic and one lane performs a single atomic for the group — thirty-two times fewer. §14 names it and Exercise 5 points at it.

9.3 — The compaction

So the count and the list come from one kernel, one thread per slot: 

StructuredBuffer<Particle>  particles : register(t0, space0);   // read-only
RWStructuredBuffer<uint>    args      : register(u0, space1);   // the draw's arguments
RWStructuredBuffer<uint>    alive     : register(u1, space1);   // the list

[numthreads(64, 1, 1)]
void main(uint3 id : SV_DispatchThreadID)
{
    const uint slot = id.x;
    if (slot >= capacity) { return; }
    const Particle p = particles[slot];
    if (!(p.age < p.life)) { return; }
    uint place;
    InterlockedAdd(args[1], 1u, place);   // args[1] is num_instances
    alive[place] = slot;
}

Three things about it. The pool is bound read-only — the compaction only looks — so it goes in the t registers and is bound with SDL_BindGPUComputeStorageBuffers, and the buffer needs the COMPUTE_STORAGE_READ usage bit. The counter is the draw's instance count: the atomic adds straight into word 1 of the SDL_GPUIndirectDrawCommand, so there is no second pass to copy it. And the list's length is whatever the count is; nothing past it is ever read, so the rest of the list is garbage and nobody cares.

Measured against the CPU after §G's ten seconds: the arguments come back as {6, 44,915, 0, 0}, and 44,915 is exactly the CPU pool's live count; sorted, the list is exactly the CPU's living slots, each once (§H).

9.4 — Somebody has to set the counter to zero

The compaction adds to args[1], so something must set it to zero first — and it cannot be the compaction. Which of its sixty-five thousand threads would do it, and how would the others know it had happened before they started adding? The order in which threads run is not yours to decide. So the reset is its own one-thread kernel, particles_clear.comp, which writes all four words — six vertices, zero instances, and the two zeros SDL_gpu.h insists on: its note on the indirect command says the built-in vertex and instance IDs are only portable when the "first" arguments are zero, and the vertex shader uses both IDs.

And it runs in its own compute pass, which is §10's subject. The buffer holding the arguments needs three usage bits: INDIRECT to be read by the draw, and both COMPUTE_STORAGE_READ and _WRITE, because an atomic reads and writes — SDL's documentation of the buffer usage flags is explicit that, unlike textures, a buffer created with both may be read and written in the same shader.

9.5 — The order, and the last bits of the picture

The list's order is whatever order the hardware served the atomics in. §H compacts one unchanged pool twice: between 44,814 and all 44,915 places held a different slot the second time, across four runs — yet about 98% of neighbouring entries are in ascending order, which is what you would see if each SIMD group's lanes took consecutive places in lane order and only the groups arrived in a different order each time. The draw does not care: the blend is addition, and addition commutes.

Except in the last bits, which is worth measuring rather than asserting, because 6.13's header for blend_add asserted the opposite. §K draws one pool three times, each after its own compaction, into the 16-bit float HDR target: about 7,000 to 9,000 of 172,800 channels differ between two draws, by at most 8 to 11 units in the last place of a half-float, while the total light agrees to one part in ten thousand (Figure 11's histogram). Floating-point addition is commutative — a + b is always exactly b + a — and it is not associative: the blender rounds after every add, so which partial sums are formed decides which roundings happen. Nothing a viewer can see moves. A golden-image test does, which is why the harness's comparisons of the picture are tolerances and its comparisons of the pool are exact. (The header comment is corrected by this lesson; §13 says where.)

10What SDL synchronises, and cycle

10.1 — Between passes: everything. Within a compute pass: nothing.

The particle frame is a chain of dependencies: each step reads the step before; the compaction reads the last step and the clear; the draw reads the compaction. On the GPU each arrow is a hazard — the reading work must not start until the writing work's results are visible — and in Vulkan and Direct3D 12 somebody must insert a barrier to say so. SDL_GPU inserts them for you, and the rule for where is short: at pass boundaries. It tracks which resources each pass uses and how, and when a pass ends it transitions them so the next pass can use them. Reading the backends at 3.4.12 confirms the shape: VULKAN_EndComputePass walks the pass's read-write buffers and textures and transitions each back to its default usage, while VULKAN_DispatchCompute records the dispatch and nothing else; D3D12_DispatchCompute likewise binds and dispatches with no barrier between dispatches.

SDL_gpu.h states the consequence in capitals under SDL_BeginGPUComputePass: reads and writes in a compute pass are not implicitly synchronised, and work that depends on a previous dispatch's output "MUST end the current compute pass and begin a new one". Hence the particle frame's shape: one compute pass per step, a pass for the clear, a pass for the compaction. Putting the clear and the compaction in one pass would race — the compaction's atomics against the clear's store of zero, in no defined order.

And on this course's machine it would work. §H does exactly the forbidden thing — clear and compact dispatched in one pass — twenty times, and gets the exact count 20 times out of 20. SDL's Metal backend opens a compute pass with computeCommandEncoder, an encoder with Metal's default settings, and on this machine that orders the two dispatches; Apple's MTLDispatchType documentation is where the serial and concurrent kinds are described. So the missing boundary is covered by behaviour SDL never promised. The harness cannot show the race on a Mac and says so; the claim that it exists elsewhere rests on SDL's contract and on the Vulkan and D3D12 source, not on an observation. This is the most dangerous kind of working there is — code that is correct on the machine it was written on and wrong on the other two backends — and it is why the frame graph of §11 derives the pass boundaries rather than trusting anybody to remember them.

10.2 — cycle, and what "undefined" costs

Lesson 4.5 met cycling as the thing that makes a per-frame upload safe. An SDL_GPU buffer is really a small ring of internal buffers; a write with cycle = true to a buffer that is still bound — referenced by work the GPU may not have finished — rotates to an unbound internal buffer instead of waiting, so this frame's write cannot land on a read last frame has not done yet. The price is in SDL_gpu.h's section on cycling: after a cycle, the resource's data is "considered to be undefined" until it is written again.

For every buffer the engine had before this lesson, that price was zero: a stream buffer is overwritten whole every frame, so its old contents were dead anyway. The particle pool is the first buffer whose contents outlive a frame — each step reads what the last one wrote — and every read-write binding at SDL_BeginGPUComputePass carries a cycle flag. §I sets it to true on the pool and runs 120 steps, one command buffer each:

  • cycle = false, submitted back to back: 38,284 alive, exactly the CPU pool.
  • cycle = true, back to back: 667 or 668.
  • cycle = true with a fence wait after every step: 334 — exactly one step's births.
  • cycle = true with SDL_WaitForGPUIdle after every step: 38,284, correct.

The third line refused a prediction. This section was drafted around the idea that cycling needs a busy GPU — that a fence wait, which proves the previous step finished, would leave nothing bound and nothing to cycle. It does not. Reading SDL's Metal backend explains why in one step: a buffer counts as bound while its reference count is non-zero, a command buffer takes a reference the first time it uses the buffer, and the reference is dropped only when SDL cleans up that command buffer — which METAL_Submit does for completed buffers during a later submit, and SDL_WaitForGPUIdle does for all of them. METAL_WaitForFences waits and cleans nothing. So at the next step's SDL_BeginGPUComputePass the pool is still referenced, and it cycles.

§I then asks which buffer each cycled step lands on, with a fresh pool and a readback after every step (Figure 12). Submitted back to back, steps 1 to 3 each start from an empty buffer, and then step 4 carries on from step 1's buffer — its survivors are serials 0–332 and its own 1,000–1,332 — step 5 from step 2's and step 6 from step 3's: the pool has become three pools, each advancing every third step. With a fence wait, every step starts from a buffer holding no live particle at all. Which buffer SDL picks is the backend's business and its timing's, which is precisely what "undefined" means; the harness asserts only that the pool is not the CPU's, and prints the pattern.

The consequence for a real frame is stronger than the harness makes it look. In the demo, the steps of one frame share one command buffer, so the second step's pass begins while the first step's pass in the same command buffer already holds a reference: cycle = true would cycle within the frame, not merely between frames. There is no frame rate, no machine and no amount of waiting short of idling the device after every pass at which the flag is right for the pool. It is wrong always — and it is right for the argument buffer's clear and for the list, which are overwritten whole. Which is to say: cycle is a buffer's load op. cycle = true is DONT_CARE; cycle = false is LOAD. The frame graph already derives a load op from whether a pass reads what it writes, and §11 teaches it to derive this one the same way.

11The frame graph learns buffers

11.1 — "The same machinery with a different descriptor"

Lesson 6.17's header listed what its graph deliberately did not do, and one line was "NO BUFFERS, ONLY TEXTURES. Every cross-pass resource in this engine is a texture. Buffers would be the same machinery with a different descriptor." The particle system is the first cross-pass buffer, so that sentence can now be checked. It turned out nine-tenths true.

What carried over unchanged is the idea the graph is built on: a resource is a sequence of versions, each produced by exactly one pass. The pool at the start of the frame is state@0; step 0 produces state@1 from it; the compaction reads state@3. Ordering (Kahn's algorithm over producer-to-consumer edges), validation (a read of a version nobody produced, two producers of one version, a cycle) and culling (a pass survives if it feeds an imported write) are all functions of versions, and none of them cared that the resource was a buffer. The buffers are imported — the pool outlives the frame, so the graph must not pool it — and an import's version 0 is its real contents, which is exactly "what the last frame left".

What did not carry over is the one-tenth, and both halves of it are the two facts of §4 and §10:

  • A compute pass is begun with its writable buffers. The graph already begins render passes for their callers, with the attachments they declared; a compute pass must be begun with the read-write buffers it declares, as an array in shader-slot order. So a buffer write declares its slot, and execute builds the array from the declarations exactly as it builds a render pass's colour targets. compile refuses slots with a gap or a repeat, because the array index is the u register and nothing else checks that the two agree.
  • A buffer's load op is cycle. The graph's three words for a texture write — discard_write, clear, keep — already say whether a pass depends on what was there. For a buffer there are two: write_buffer (overwrites, so cycle = true) and keep_buffer (reads what is there, so cycle = false, and the pass is ordered after the version's producer).

Plus the two things SDL_GPU forbids, which the graph now refuses at compile time rather than letting the driver refuse them halfway through a frame: a render pass that writes a buffer (graphics stages cannot write storage) and a compute pass with an attachment.

11.2 — The particle frame, declared

The demo's frame, minus the lines that fill in the callbacks' contexts: 

const fg_buffer state0 = fg.import_buffer("particle state", pool, pool_bytes);
const fg_buffer alive0 = fg.import_buffer("alive list", list, list_bytes);
const fg_buffer args0  = fg.import_buffer("draw args", args, 16);

fg_buffer state = state0;
for (int k = 0; k < steps; ++k)
{
    const int pass = fg.add_compute_pass(names[k], &exec_step, &step_ctx[k]);
    state = fg.keep_buffer(pass, state, 0);             // read-modify-write
}

const int clear = fg.add_compute_pass("clear args", &exec_clear, &particles);
const fg_buffer args1 = fg.write_buffer(clear, args0, 0);          // overwritten

const int compact = fg.add_compute_pass("compact", &exec_compact, &compact_ctx);
fg.read_buffer(compact, state);
const fg_buffer args2  = fg.keep_buffer(compact, args1, 0);        // accumulated
const fg_buffer alive1 = fg.write_buffer(compact, alive0, 1);      // overwritten

const int scene = fg.add_pass("scene", &exec_scene, &scene_ctx);
const fg_texture hdr1   = fg.clear(scene, hdr0, dark);
const fg_texture depth1 = fg.clear_depth(scene, depth0, 1.0f);

const int sparks = fg.add_pass("sparks", &exec_sparks, &spark_ctx);
fg.read_buffer(sparks, state);
fg.read_buffer(sparks, alive1);
fg.read_buffer(sparks, args2);                                    // the indirect arguments
(void)fg.keep(sparks, hdr1);                                      // additive: the scene is an operand
(void)fg.keep_depth(sparks, depth1);                              // tested, never written

Nothing there says what runs first, which pass may cycle what, or what array any compute pass is begun with. §J compiles the harness's version of it (three steps and no scene) and reads back the deduction: the schedule is step 0, step 1, step 2, clear args, compact, particles, and the derived flags are cycle no for every step's pool and for the compaction's arguments, cycle yes for the clear's arguments and the compaction's list — the four values §10 argued for, none of them written down. Figure 13 draws the demo's seven passes against its five resources.

Then §J does what 6.17 did for textures: it records the same frame by hand — gpu_particles::simulate and a hand-begun render pass — and compares. The pool after the declared frame equals the pool after the hand-recorded one byte for byte, and both equal the CPU's three steps. The two HDR images differ in the last bits of about 4,000 of 172,800 channels, at most 8 to 17 half-float units, with the total light equal to a part in ten thousand — the atomics' order, as §9.5 predicts, and nothing else.

And the four refusals, each with its control: a render pass that writes a buffer, a compute pass that clears a colour attachment, read-write slots 0 and 2, and two buffers in slot 0 all fail compile with a message naming the pass; slots 0 and 1 compile. One more property falls out of culling with no new code: declare a draw that feeds nothing — into a transient texture no one reads — and the graph culls the draw and keeps the step, because the step writes an imported buffer and an import's value outlives the frame. The simulation advances whether or not anybody looks at it, which for a particle system is the right answer.

11.3 — A cost the additivity check caught

The first version of these changes answered "is this a read?" and "is this imported?" with small helper functions, called in the graph's two innermost loops — producer_of and the two-producer check, both quadratic in passes and in accesses. The harnesses link the engine as the default build compiles it, with no optimisation, where an inline helper is a real call; and 6.17's own harness, rerun unchanged for §13's additivity check, reported its steady-state compile at 13.5 µs where it had been 8.1. The fix stores a one-byte writes flag on each access when it is declared — a load, as cheap as the single comparison it replaced — and repacks the three new fields into four bytes of the record. Rerun: 7.7 to 8.7 µs. Nothing about the answer had changed; a frame graph rebuilt every frame is exactly the code where "nothing changed but it is 60% slower" matters.

11.4 — Where the graph stops

The demo is the first program in the course whose frame is declared rather than recorded — and it declares only part of it. The steps, the clear, the compaction, the scene and the sparks go through the graph; 6.13's bloom and the display pass (the tonemap and 6.18's overlay) are recorded after execute, by hand, exactly as the sandbox records them. The line is where it is because those two already have owners: gpu_post_stack::render_bloom begins its own eleven passes, and the display pass belongs to the swapchain. Declaring them would mean rewriting the post stack's interface, which 6.17's harness did for itself in about sixty lines and which belongs to whoever next changes the post stack — not to a lesson about particles. The HDR target is imported, so the graph stores it for the bloom to read; the depth buffer is the graph's own, and the sparks' pass is the last to touch it, so the graph derives DONT_CARE for it.

12Implementation

12.1 — The specification: particles.hpp

Start on the CPU, with no SDL_GPU anywhere: the record, the hash, the clock, the step. Every function has a twin in particles_step.comp.hlsl, and the two are written in the same order of operations, because a floating-point expression is not a mathematical one — a compiler may not rearrange what the source did not arrange, and keeping the texts parallel is what makes the harness's comparison mean "the GPU did what the CPU did" rather than "two similar programs gave similar numbers".

The uniform block is the file's central idea. step_uniforms is nine 16-byte rows, built once per step by make_step_uniforms, and read unchanged by both the CPU's step_slot and the kernel: 

struct step_uniforms
{
    vec3 origin{};    float h = 0.0f;                    // row 0
    vec3 axis{};      float one_minus_cos_cone = 0.0f;   // row 1  (§5.5)
    vec3 tangent{};   float speed_min = 0.0f;            // row 2  (the cone's frame, computed once)
    vec3 bitangent{}; float speed_span = 0.0f;           // row 3
    vec3 gravity{};   float inv_drag_h = 1.0f;           // row 4  (1 / (1 + k h), §7.2)
    float life_min, life_span, ground, restitution;      // row 5
    float keep, drag, carry, inv_rate;                   // row 6  (1 − friction; §6.4's clock)
    Uint32 first, count, mask, seed;                     // row 7  (the emission window)
    Uint32 capacity, pad0, pad1, pad2;                   // row 8
};

Every number in it that is the same for every particle — the cone's cap height and frame, the drag factor, the friction complement — is computed here, once, in C++. So the CPU reference does not compute its own 1/(1 + kh): it reads the same float the GPU reads, and a disagreement between the processors can only come from arithmetic that follows. That is also why it is 144 bytes rather than the 80 of the emitter's own fields — and 144 bytes a step is still the CPU's entire contribution.

step_slot is one thread's work, and the CPU pool is a loop over it: 

void step_slot(particle& p, Uint32 slot, const step_uniforms& u)
{
    const Uint32 d = (slot - u.first) & u.mask;         // distance round the ring (§6.2)
    if (d < u.count)
    {
        p = spawn_particle(u.first + d, birth_age(d, u.carry, u.inv_rate, u.h), u);
        return;
    }
    if (!is_alive(p)) { return; }                       // dead stays dead, byte for byte
    p.previous = p.position;                            // §7.5
    integrate_particle(p, u, u.h, u.inv_drag_h);        // §7.1–7.3
    p.age = p.age + u.h;
}

Dead particles are left exactly as they died, not zeroed — which the harness relies on when it compares whole buffers, and which saves the kernel a store for the one slot in three that is dead.

12.2 — The kernel

particles_step.comp.hlsl is that function transliterated: the same struct of three rows, the same cbuffer of nine at b0, space2, pcg_hash and unit_float character for character, and a main that is step_slot with the tail check in front. The pool is RWStructuredBuffer<Particle> at u0, space1. Read the two files side by side; the listing is in §15.

12.3 — Loading a compute pipeline

gpu_compute_pipeline::load follows gpu_shader::load step for step: choose the format this device accepts (MSL here, entry point main0), read the code, read the reflection with the new parse_compute_reflection, refuse to guess if it is not a compute reflection, then fill SDL_GPUComputePipelineCreateInfo — six counts and three thread dimensions, all read from the file — and name the pipeline at creation through SDL_PROP_GPU_COMPUTEPIPELINE_CREATE_NAME_STRING, as 4.9 taught every resource to be named. groups_for_items(n) sizes a dispatch from the pipeline's own threadcount_x, so a kernel whose group size changes cannot be dispatched with the old one.

12.4 — gpu_particles: three buffers and four recordings

create makes the pool, the list and the arguments with the usage bits §8.2 and §9.4 argued for, loads the three kernels by name, builds the draw pipeline — no vertex input, additive, depth-tested without writes — and then zeroes the pool with one upload, because SDL_gpu.h promises nothing about a new buffer's contents, and "whatever the allocator last held" is a pool of particles with random ages, some alive, drawn on the first frame at random positions. A zeroed record is a dead particle (§4.1), so the pool starts empty by construction.

Then four recording functions, one per kind of pass, and none of them begins a pass — the shape 6.18's overlay settled on, made non-negotiable here by §4.4: whoever begins a compute pass must know which buffers it writes, so each function's comment says exactly which buffer goes in which slot and whether it may cycle: 

void record_step   (cb, compute_pass, const step_uniforms&);   // slot 0: state, cycle = false
void record_clear  (compute_pass);                              // slot 0: args,  cycle may be true
void record_compact(cb, compute_pass, SDL_GPUBuffer* state);    // slots: args (false), alive (true)
void record_draw   (cb, render_pass, const particle_draw_uniforms&, SDL_GPUBuffer* state);

and simulate / count_living, which begin those passes themselves, for a program with no frame graph and for the harness's hand-recorded control. The draw is one call, SDL_DrawGPUPrimitivesIndirect(pass, args, 0, 1), after binding the pool and the list to the vertex stage and pushing the camera.

12.5 — The frame graph

frame_graph.hpp gains fg_buffer — fg_texture's twin, a different type so a buffer cannot be passed where a texture was meant — and import_buffer, add_compute_pass, read_buffer, write_buffer and keep_buffer. A buffer is a resource slot like any other, with its SDL_GPUBuffer* where a texture keeps its pointer; two new uses, buffer_read and buffer_write, join sample, colour and depth. In compile, the store-op loop derives cycle = (init == discard) for a buffer write and continues, and a new validation block enforces §11.1's rules. In execute, a compute pass gathers its declared writes into an SDL_GPUStorageBufferReadWriteBinding array indexed by slot, begins the pass, and hands the callback ctx.compute. Every texture-only graph takes exactly the path it took before, which §13 checks.

12.6 — The demo, and the fixed step on the GPU

demos/particles is an engine::app on surface::gpu. The one piece of it worth reading closely is how a fixed step reaches the GPU: 

void on_fixed_step(float h) override
{
    // (abridged: the listing adds the pause, the --shot guard and the step timer)
    if (cpu_mode_) { (void)cpu_pool_.step(emitter_, h); return; }   // the "before"

    // No command buffer exists yet, so the step is RECORDED, not run.
    const emission_window w = clock_.advance(emitter_.rate, h, particles_.capacity());
    steps_[step_count_++].u = make_step_uniforms(emitter_, w, h, particles_.capacity());
}

and on_frame declares one compute pass per recorded step (at most eight — Lesson 1.4's spiral-of-death cap), then the rest of the frame, with alpha in the draw's uniforms. Both paths advance the same emission clock at the same steps, so they emit the same particles at the same times; the CPU path adds one line before the graph, upload_cpu_state, and hands the graph the uploaded buffer instead of the GPU's pool. [C] switches live, and the HUD reports what the CPU path costs.

13The instruments: two processors held to one specification

13.1 — What must be exact, and what cannot be

§G runs the CPU pool and the GPU pool from the same empty state through the same 600 uniform blocks — ten simulated seconds — and compares them particle by particle at seven checkpoints. Before looking, it is worth deciding what "agree" can mean, because the answer is different for different parts of the record.
