  • Integers must agree exactly. Serials, the hash, the emission window, the ring: integer arithmetic has one right answer. After ten seconds every serial is in the same slot on both processors, and 1,048,576 hashes match bit for bit.
  • Floats cannot, in general. The kernel calls sin, cos and sqrt, which the GPU approximates; its compiler may fuse a multiply and an add that C++ rounds twice. After one step, the 333 new particles' lives are identical — a multiply-add of exact values — but only 93 of their 333 velocities are bit-identical, the worst 4 units in the last place.
  • So floats are held to a tolerance, and the tolerance is stated. After ten seconds, 44,889 of 44,915 live particles are within a micrometre of their twin and the worst is 1.38 µm; the worst at any checkpoint was 1.67 µm. Only 5,264 — 12% — are bit-identical.
  • Which particles are alive must agree exactly anyway, because the count drives a draw. It does: zero disagreements at every checkpoint, and the GPU's count equals the CPU's, 44,915.

That last line refused a prediction too, and the refusal is instructive. The expectation was that the floor would be where the two processors part: a particle a few ULPs above the plane on one and a few below on the other bounces a step earlier on one of them, and from then on they are centimetres apart. Over ten seconds, 44,915 living particles and several bounces each, it never happened — no live particle is even a millimetre from its twin. The floor turns out to be a contraction: a bounce sets the height to exactly ground on both processors, so whatever vertical error had accumulated is discarded at every impact. Divergence would need a particle to end a step within a few ULPs of the plane, which is a one-in-millions coincidence per impact.

13.2 — Which CPU is the reference?

There is a harder question underneath §13.1: the CPU reference is compiled too. The harness links the engine library, and the default build compiles it with no optimisation while a Release build optimises it — and the optimiser may fuse a multiply and an add in the reference exactly as the GPU's compiler may. §G dumps the CPU pool's bytes after ten seconds from each build and compares them: 897 of 44,915 live particles differ between the debug and Release builds of the same C++, the worst by 0.60 µm, with no disagreement about which are alive. So a bit-exact float reference does not exist even on one processor unless the compiler is forbidden to contract, and the honest contract for float state is a tolerance: exact integers, exact alive/dead decisions, positions within a stated number of micrometres.

13.3 — The budget

§L times both paths against a Release library — which the harness's build script insists on naming, because a harness's own -O2 never reaches the library it links, and the default library's CPU step is six times slower (21 ns a slot against 3.5). The CPU step costs 3.3 to 3.6 ns a slot, flat from 16,384 to a million — the loop streams through memory in order, which is the access pattern a CPU is best at. The upload costs about 0.14 ms per megabyte plus about 0.14 ms of submission; it overtakes the step at every size and reaches 6.87 ms at a million. The GPU step, sixty steps in one command buffer so the launch cost is shared, costs 0.31 to 0.79 ns a slot including that launch — the smallest pool pays most per slot because 16,384 particles do not fill the GPU (Figure 15).

Two honest limits on those numbers. SDL_GPU has no GPU timestamp queries, so the GPU column is wall-clock time around a submit and a fence — an upper bound on the GPU's work, and the reason sixty steps are timed together. And this machine's GPU shares memory with its CPU; on a discrete card the upload also crosses PCIe, which makes the CPU path worse, not better.

13.4 — Twenty-seven harnesses that must not move

This lesson is inserted into a published sequence, so it must be additive: every measurement a later lesson made must come out the same with it as without it. Before the first edit, every Module 6 and 7 harness — twenty-seven of them, 6.1 to 6.18 with 6.17b, and 7.1 to 7.8 — was run and its output kept; after the lesson, they were run again. Every one still exits 0. Every differing line is a timing, a timestamp in a log line, the interleaving of standard output with standard error, or a heap pointer — with one exception, which was a cost rather than a result, and which §11.3 describes and fixed: 6.17's frame-graph compile, 8.1 µs before and 13.5 µs after the first version, 7.7 to 8.7 after the fix. The reference render is still E917C06C.

And the correction promised in §9.5: the doc comment on pipeline_desc::blend_add said additive blending is order-independent because "addition is commutative and associative". Commutative is right and is all the no-sort argument needs; associative is not, and §K measured what that means. The comment now says so, in the header and in the three earlier lessons' listings that carry it (6.13, 6.14 and 6.16), and 6.13's prose carries a note.

14The ninety-percent picture

This is a complete GPU particle system of the simplest useful kind. Here is the rest of the field, and what each part would cost this engine.

  • Sorting. Additive sparks need no sort. Smoke, dust and anything drawn with 6.11's over operator do — back to front, per frame, on the GPU, which means a parallel sort (bitonic, or a radix sort) of tens of thousands of keys: another set of compute passes, each depending on the last. Or order-independent transparency, which avoids the sort at the price of memory per pixel.
  • A dead list instead of a ring. Gareth Thomas's GDC 2014 talk describes the design most production systems use: a stack of free slots that births pop and deaths push, so no living particle is ever overwritten and an emitter can burst. It costs two atomics per particle per frame and a CPU reference that can only check counts, not slots (Exercise 5).
  • Wave intrinsics. §9.2's atomics can be cut thirty-two-fold by counting a SIMD group's survivors with WaveActiveCountBits and one atomic per group. That needs Shader Model 6 wave operations through every hop of this toolchain — HLSL, SPIR-V subgroups, MSL SIMD-group functions — and is left as research: ⚠ VERIFY that glslc and SPIRV-Cross carry them before depending on it.
  • Colliding with the world. The only thing a particle knows about is one plane. Colliding with the scene's depth buffer — sampling it in the step kernel and bouncing off whatever the camera can see — is cheap and convincing and wrong off-screen (Exercise 4). A signed distance field of the level is right everywhere and costs a 3D texture.
  • Lighting, and sparks as lights. The sparks emit and are not lit, which suits sparks. Smoke must be lit — 6.17b's lamps through a volume — and a shower of sparks would, in a real scene, light the floor under it: the brightest few thousand as 6.17b's point lights, which is what clustered shading (6.17b §12) exists for.
  • Soft particles. A billboard crossing the floor is cut by a hard line where it meets the depth buffer. Fading each fragment by its distance to the depth behind it removes the line, and needs the depth buffer as a sampled texture in the draw — a declaration the frame graph already knows how to make.
  • Async compute. On hardware with a separate compute queue the particle steps could overlap the previous frame's post-processing. SDL_GPU exposes one queue, and 6.17's graph says so in its own header.
  • Indirect dispatch. The step runs over every slot, dead or alive. A system that steps only the living would dispatch ceil(count / 64) groups — a number only the GPU knows — through SDL_DispatchGPUComputeIndirect, the dispatch twin of §9's indirect draw.

15Complete code listings

Every file this lesson changed or created, in full, as it stands at the end of 6.18b — the tree a student has after 6.18, plus this lesson and nothing later. 16Build & run

Three new translation units, four compute shaders and two graphics shaders, and a new demo. add_hlsl_shader has accepted compute as a stage since Lesson 4.3 wrote it in a comment; this is the first time anything passes it. The build compiles each kernel to SPIR-V, MSL and (with a DXC-enabled shadercross) DXIL, plus the nine-number reflection. 

# Linux / macOS
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
cmake --build build -j

# Windows (MSVC)
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo

Then the harness, and — separately — its timings against a Release library:

sh scratch/build_verify_618b.sh                         # every check, as configured
cmake -S . -B build-rel -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-rel --target engine
ENGINE_BUILD=build-rel ENGINE_CFLAGS="-O2 -DNDEBUG" sh scratch/build_verify_618b.sh   # §L

§L times particle_pool::step, which lives in libengine.a, and a harness's own -O2 never reaches a library it links. The script prints which library it linked and its build type, and §L says in its own output whether its CPU column may be quoted: against the default, unoptimised library the step measures about 21 ns a slot, against Release about 3.5.

And the demo:

cd build/demos
./particles                      # the fountain, simulated on the GPU
./particles --cpu                # the same fountain, simulated on the CPU and uploaded
./particles --count 262144       # a bigger pool (rounded up to a power of two)
./particles --shot out.ppm       # one frame, 2.5 s in, no window
./particles --log gpu=info       # then press [G]: the frame graph's deduction, printed

Keys: [C] switches between the GPU and the CPU simulation (each restarts from an empty pool), [B] toggles the bloom, [Space] pauses the emitter so the last sparks can be watched dying, and [G] dumps the frame graph once.

Expected result

The harness ends with 71 checks, 0 failure(s). It reports the device it found (GPU: driver 'metal' on a Mac) before the device sections; with no GPU it runs §B and §D–§F and skips the rest. Read §G's table — ten seconds of 0 alive/dead disagreements and a worst distance in micrometres — and §I's two six-step traces, which are the most instructive twenty lines in the lesson. The numbers that come from the hardware's scheduling — §H's lost updates, the list's order, the images' last bits, §I's back-to-back count — differ from run to run, and the checks on them are written as bounds.

The demo opens a 1280 × 720 window on a dark floor under a cool moonlight. A fountain of warm sparks rises from the floor, white at its core where thousands overlap, cooling to orange as they fall, blooming where they are densest and bouncing into a spray across the floor. A metal torus stands on edge to the right, and the sparks that fall behind it are hidden by it — the depth test — while it hides nothing it should not. The HUD says 65536 sparks, simulated on the GPU and that the count never leaves the GPU. Press [C]: the fountain restarts, looks the same, and the HUD now reports a CPU step (about 1.4 ms in a default build, 0.23 in Release) and 3.00 MB uploaded every frame. --shot produces Figure 16. Two shots are not byte-identical — about 1,700 of 2.76 million bytes differ between two runs of the same binary, never by more than one code — because the compaction's order differs (§9.5); a GPU shot and a CPU shot differ by the same amount, not more.

17Common pitfalls & debugging

The fountain keeps only its newest sparks, or turns into several fountains taking turns

Symptom: a few hundred particles near the emitter and nothing older; or a pool that seems to advance in fits, with particles from several "generations" interleaved.
Cause: the pool's read-write binding has cycle = true. The step reads what the last step wrote, and a cycled buffer's contents are undefined — SDL hands the pass another internal buffer, empty or holding an older history (§10.2).
Fix: cycle = false for any buffer a pass reads and writes. Declare it with keep_buffer and the frame graph derives it.

Particles fly off in wrong directions at wrong speeds, differently for each one

Symptom: every particle is plausible and every one is wrong; the error grows along the buffer.
Cause: a storage struct with a float3 followed by another float3. C++ puts the second at byte 12, the SPIR-V path at 16, so the stride differs and every record after the first is read from the wrong offset (§4.2).
Fix: rows of float3 + one scalar, or float4s; name any padding explicitly on both sides; static_assert every offset in C++ and read one record back from the GPU once.

The kernel runs and its uniforms are all zero

Symptom: particles spawn at the origin with no velocity, or nothing ever spawns.
Cause: the cbuffer is declared at b0, space1 — a vertex shader's uniform space — or space3. A compute shader's uniforms are b[n], space2 (§4.4).
Fix: register(b0, space2), and check the reflection: "uniform_buffers": 1 is necessary but not sufficient, because a wrong space still reflects a uniform block.

The first frame is full of sparks in random places

Symptom: a burst of particles everywhere on the first frame, never repeated.
Cause: the pool was not zeroed. SDL promises nothing about a new buffer's contents, and random ages and lives make some records alive.
Fix: upload zeros once at creation, as gpu_particles::create does. A zeroed record is dead by construction (§4.1).

Nothing is drawn, or everything is drawn twice, on Windows or Linux only

Symptom: correct on a Mac; no particles, or a flickering count, on Vulkan or Direct3D 12.
Cause: the clear and the compaction are in one compute pass. Metal's serial encoder orders the two dispatches; Vulkan and D3D12 do not, and the atomics race the clear (§10.1).
Fix: one pass per dependent dispatch. Declared through the frame graph, a pass that reads a version another pass produced is ordered after it and in its own pass by construction.

The count is a few hundred when it should be tens of thousands

Symptom: a sparse fountain; the draw's instance count varies wildly frame to frame.
Cause: the compaction increments with args[1] = args[1] + 1. Lanes read the same value together, and most increments are lost (§9.2: 296 to 509 of 1,048,576).
Fix: InterlockedAdd(args[1], 1u, place), and use place as the index into the list.

The draw crashes the device or draws nothing, and the buffer looks right

Symptom: validation errors naming the indirect buffer, or a device loss.
Cause: the arguments buffer lacks SDL_GPU_BUFFERUSAGE_INDIRECT, or lacks COMPUTE_STORAGE_READ beside _WRITE for the atomic's read; or first_vertex/first_instance are not zero while the vertex shader uses the built-in IDs.
Fix: all three usage bits (§9.4), and a clear kernel that writes all four words.

The fountain comes out in horizontal layers

Symptom: shells a step's travel apart, most visible with a narrow speed range.
Cause: every birth of a step is spawned at age zero at the emitter.
Fix: birth_age: each birth advanced by its own age within the step (§6.4).

Sparks vanish in mid-air at a fixed height

Symptom: the fountain is truncated; its top looks cut off.
Cause: the ring overwrites living particles — the pool is smaller than rate × longest life.
Fix: capacity / rate > life_max. At 32,768 slots and 20,000 a second, 76.4% of particles died early (§6.3).

A streak across the screen at every birth

Symptom: thin lines from random points to the emitter, one frame long.
Cause: a respawned slot keeps the old tenant's previous, and the draw interpolates between two different particles.
Fix: set previous to the emitter at spawn (§7.5).

Sparks pop in and out of view where they cross each other

Symptom: dark holes in the fountain that move every frame.
Cause: the particle pipeline writes depth, so each spark occludes those behind it, and the list's order — which decides who was first — changes every frame.
Fix: depth test on, depth write off (§8.3).

SDL_CreateGPUDevice failed: Video subsystem not initialized in a headless shot

Symptom: the demo runs in a window and fails with --shot.
Cause: surface::headless leaves the video subsystem uninitialised, and SDL_GPU needs it with or without a window.
Fix: .extra_subsystems = SDL_INIT_VIDEO in the app_config for the shot, as the demo does.

The frame graph refuses to compile the frame

Symptom: compile returns false and the log names a pass.
Cause: one of §11.1's rules: a render pass declared a buffer write, a compute pass declared an attachment, or a compute pass's read-write slots have a gap or a repeat.
Fix: the message names the pass and the slot. Slots are the shader's u registers, 0 to n − 1.

18Exercises

1 — Wind, derived implicitly (guided)

Add a wind velocity w to the emitter: linear drag pulls a particle toward the air's velocity rather than toward rest, dv/dt = g − k(v − w). Derive the implicit step, add w to step_uniforms on both sides without breaking the row rule, and keep §G green.

Solution sketch: solving v′ = v + (g − k(v′ − w))h gives v′ = (v + (g + kw)h) / (1 + kh) — the same factor, with gravity replaced by g + kw. So the cheapest change is not a new row at all: fold kw into the gravity row on the CPU, in make_step_uniforms, and the kernel does not change. The one catch is the birth's pre-age step, which uses its own drag factor; it must use the same folded acceleration. A particle then drifts toward w with time constant 1/k — 2.5 s at the demo's k = 0.4, so a 3 s spark ends about 70% of the way to the wind's speed.

2 — A burst (guided)

Make [R] emit 20,000 sparks at once on top of the steady stream. Decide what the burst's births should look like in time, what happens when a burst exceeds the pool, and what the ring does to the sparks already alive.

Solution sketch: a burst is one window of count births in one step, advancing the clock's serials by count; emission_clock::advance already caps a window at the capacity, so a burst of 100,000 into 65,536 slots emits 65,536 and says nothing — log it instead. Give the burst inv_rate = 0 and every birth has age h: born together, which for an explosion is correct, and is exactly the shell §6.4 removed for a steady stream. The ring's price is the real lesson: 20,000 births replace the 20,000 oldest slots, alive or not. With the default fountain those slots hold the sparks born 2.3 to 3.3 seconds earlier; a spark born t seconds ago is alive while its life, uniform on [1.5, 3], exceeds t, which over that window averages to about 17% — so the burst kills some 3,500 of the fountain's 45,000 sparks early, at the top of their arcs. Compute it for a burst of 40,000, and that is the strongest argument for Exercise 5's dead list.

3 — Show the count without a stall (guided)

The HUD in GPU mode says the count never leaves the GPU. Put it on the HUD anyway, without ever waiting for the GPU: read it a few frames late.

Solution sketch: after the compaction each frame, record SDL_DownloadFromGPUBuffer of the 16-byte arguments into one of three download transfer buffers, round-robin, and keep the frame's fence from SDL_SubmitGPUCommandBufferAndAcquireFence. At the start of each frame, for any slot whose fence SDL_QueryGPUFence reports signalled, map the buffer, read word 1, and release the fence. The HUD shows a count two or three frames old, and the frame never blocks — which is the general shape of every GPU-to-CPU readback a real engine does (occlusion queries, picking, auto-exposure). Check it against --cpu mode's exact count: in steady state they agree within the births of the frames in between.

4 — Collide with the depth buffer (engine challenge)

Make sparks bounce off the torus and anything else the camera can see. In the step kernel, project a particle with the camera's clip_from_world, sample the scene's depth there, and if the particle has passed behind the surface by less than a thickness, reflect its velocity about the surface normal.

Solution sketch: the depth must be a sampled texture in a compute pass — bound with SDL_BindGPUComputeSamplers, t0, space0 before the read-only buffers — so its format must support sampling (6.8's supported_shadow_format asks), and it must be last frame's depth: this frame's is drawn after the steps. Import it into the frame graph so it is stored, and declare sample on it in each step pass. The normal comes from the depth's neighbours: reconstruct three world positions and cross their differences. Then face the honest limits: a particle behind the torus from the camera's view cannot collide with its back, one off-screen collides with nothing, and a thickness too large makes sparks bounce off the air in front of silhouettes. Screen-space collision is a trick that looks right where the camera is looking, which is why it is popular and why a signed distance field is what replaces it.

5 — A dead list instead of a ring (engine challenge)

Replace the ring with the design from Gareth Thomas's GDC 2014 talk: a stack of free slot indices. Births pop from it, deaths push to it, and no living particle is ever overwritten. Keep a CPU twin and decide what it can still check.

Solution sketch: a dead buffer of indices and a counter, initialised to all slots. The step becomes two kernels in two passes: one that ages and integrates the living and, for each particle that dies, does InterlockedAdd(dead_count, 1, i) and writes its slot to dead[i]; one that runs a thread per birth, does InterlockedAdd(dead_count, -1, j) on a signed counter and spawns into dead[j - 1] if j > 0 — a birth that finds the stack empty has driven the counter negative, and a later pass must clamp it back to zero, which is a third dependency and a third pass. Which slot a birth lands in now depends on the order of the atomics, so the CPU twin can check the count alive and the multiset of serials alive — both still exact — but no longer slot by slot. Measure the cost against the ring at 65,536 and 1,048,576: two atomics per particle per step against none. Then make it cheaper with a wave-level reduction, after the ⚠ VERIFY in §14.

19Recap & next — and Module 6's project tree

The engine can compute. A compute pipeline is loaded from code and a nine-number reflection, run as a grid of thread groups whose ragged tail every kernel guards, and handed read-write storage buffers when its pass begins. The particle record is three 16-byte rows because two compilers read anything else two ways — measured, not assumed. Randomness is a hash of a particle's name, PCG's, bit-identical on both processors, where the three popular alternatives are correlated, short of bits, or not even one function. An emitter is a clock that keeps its fraction and a ring that needs no atomics, with each birth placed where it belongs in its step; the step is semi-implicit Euler with implicit drag and a floor whose bounces are as accurate as the step allows; and the particles are drawn as billboards with no vertex buffer, added to the HDR light, tested against the scene.

The count of the living is produced by an atomic and consumed by an indirect draw without the CPU ever learning it, and the draw's order changes every frame in the last bits and nowhere else. SDL synchronises passes and nothing within them, and cycle turned out to be a buffer's load op — wrong for the pool in every frame, as §I's traces show. The frame graph learned buffers and compute passes, and derives that flag and the read-write bindings from the same declarations it derived load ops from; the demo is the first program whose frame is declared. And the GPU was held to a CPU specification with honest tolerances: exact where the arithmetic is integer, within 1.67 µm where it is not, and the reference itself no more exact than that across its own builds.

Next: 7.1 — Euler Angles and Their Pathologies. Module 6 ends here with a renderer that lights, shadows, blooms, writes text and now computes. Everything it has rotated so far — the camera's orbit, the torus standing on edge, a light's cone axis — was rotated by a matrix written down whole or by look_at. Module 7 asks what a rotation is, starting with the three angles everyone reaches for first and the way they fail: two axes that line up, a degree of freedom that disappears, and a camera that cannot turn.

20Further reading

  • Mark Jarzynski and Marc Olano, "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering", JCGT 9(3), 2020 — a range of hashes measured for quality with TestU01 and for speed on GPUs, and the recommendation this lesson follows. Nathan Reed's post on the paper is the short version, with the code.
  • Melissa O'Neill, PCG, A Family of Better Random Number Generators — where the output permutation comes from, and why an LCG's low bits need one.
  • Tom Duff et al., "Building an Orthonormal Basis, Revisited", JCGT 6(1), 2017 — the branch-free tangent frame make_step_uniforms uses, and the precision bug in the version it replaced.
  • Gareth Thomas, "Compute-based GPU Particle Systems", GDC 2014 — dead lists, sorting on the GPU and indirect dispatch: the ninety-percent picture's other ten per cent, from AMD.
  • Moonside Games, "SDL GPU Concepts: Cycling" — the post SDL_gpu.h itself points to on cycling, and the clearest statement of when it is safe.
  • SDL_gpu.h at release-3.4.12 — the resource layouts above SDL_CreateGPUComputePipeline and SDL_CreateGPUShader, SDL_BeginGPUComputePass's note on synchronisation, the buffer usage flags, and SDL_GPUIndirectDrawCommand; rendered on the SDL3 wiki, for example SDL_BeginGPUComputePass and SDL_DrawGPUPrimitivesIndirect.
  • SDL's own backends at the same tag — src/gpu/vulkan/SDL_gpu_vulkan.c (VULKAN_EndComputePass), src/gpu/metal/SDL_gpu_metal.m (METAL_INTERNAL_PrepareBufferForWrite, METAL_Submit) — the only place §10's mechanisms are written down.
  • Microsoft, InterlockedAdd and SV_DispatchThreadID — the atomic and the thread IDs, in HLSL's own words.
  • Apple, MTLDispatchType — serial and concurrent compute encoders, and why the race of §10.1 does not happen on a Mac.
  • Khronos, Vulkan Synchronization Examples — the barriers SDL writes for you, compute-to-compute and compute-to-indirect-draw among them.
  • Glenn Fiedler, "Fix Your Timestep!" — the fixed step and interpolation that §2 and §12.6 carry onto the GPU.
